topic: ripening small tommes in a stone cellar: rind moulds, cellar humidity and the pace of ripening

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: rejestrator wilgotnosci

base: I ripen small tommes in a stone cellar and the rinds have started behaving oddly.
An older wheel from the spring make sits on the top shelf and looks perfect.
A humidity logger hangs by the door and records the cellar every quarter of an hour.
The young tomme has grown a patch of black mould where it touches the board.
Should I wash that patch off, or turn the wheel and leave it to dry?
Brush it off dry first, because washing drives spores into the rind you are building.
Black mould at the board means the underside never dries between one turning and the next.
Turn daily for the first fortnight and wipe the board each time with a dry cloth.
A settled grey rind will crowd the black out once it has properly taken hold.
I turned daily for two weeks and the black patch has not come back at all.
A soft grey coat is spreading over the whole wheel, exactly as you had described.
The humidity logger shows ninety four percent by day and rather more at night.
The older wheel never grew a coat this thick, though it sat in the same cellar.
Is that reading too high, or does a young tomme need more moisture than an old one?
Ninety four is high for a tomme, which likes about ninety percent at this stage.
Too much moisture gives you a thick soft coat that later slips off the paste.
Crack the door for an hour each morning and let the cellar breathe a little.
The older wheel grew a thin rind because it ripened through a drier part of the year.
Opening the door each morning brought the reading down to about ninety one percent.
The grey coat has firmed up and now feels dry and slightly furred to the hand.
Underneath, though, the paste near the rind has gone noticeably softer than the centre.
Is that normal ripening from outside inward, or a sign that something is going wrong?
That is normal, because the moulds on the rind break the paste down from outside.
A soft band under the rind widens slowly and should reach the centre by spring.
Worry only if the band smells of ammonia or turns runny against the rind itself.
Otherwise let the wheel take its own time and resist cutting it too early.
The band has widened evenly and there is no smell of ammonia anywhere on the wheel.
I cut one tomme at ten weeks and the paste was smooth right through the middle.
The flavour is mild, though, and rather flat compared with cheeses I have bought.
Would longer ripening deepen it, or does that depend on the milk more than the cellar?
Longer ripening will deepen it, but the milk sets the ceiling you can ever reach.
Late summer milk from grazed cows carries far more flavour than winter milk on hay.
Keep a few wheels to four months and taste them beside the ten week ones.
You will learn more from that comparison than from any change to the cellar itself.
The four month wheels are much deeper and one has developed a faint nutty sweetness.
Two of them cracked slightly across the top, which spoiled the look if not the taste.
The cracks appeared during the cold spell when I let the cellar drop below eight degrees.
Should I heat the cellar in winter, or simply accept a few cracked wheels each year?
Do not heat it, because steady cold is worth far more than a perfect surface.
Cracks come from a sudden change rather than from cold itself, in almost every cellar.
Hang a heavy curtain inside the door so the cold arrives slowly and leaves slowly.
Then let the season do what it likes and keep the wheels turning as usual.
